paragraphs.heading: A liquid layer deep down
paragraphs.text: The outer core is a layer of fluid, mostly iron and nickel, roughly 2,260 km thick. It lies beneath the mantle and above the solid inner core. Its top, the core-mantle boundary, is about 2,889 km below the surface, and its bottom, at the inner core boundary, is about 5,150 km down. Unlike the inner core, it is liquid.

paragraphs.heading: Why it stays liquid
paragraphs.text: The main evidence comes from seismology: seismic shear waves do not pass through the outer core. Its makeup is close to the inner core's, but the pressure is not great enough to hold it solid. Its outer edge sits about 3,483 km from Earth's center, give or take 5 km. Temperatures are estimated at about 3,000 to 4,500 K in its outer part and 4,000 to 8,000 K near the inner core.

paragraphs.heading: The source of Earth's magnetism
paragraphs.text: Models show that its high temperature makes the outer core a runny fluid that churns turbulently. Its fluid flows at speeds of up to about 1 millimeter each second, or about 30 kilometers in a year. In dynamo theory, swirling eddy currents in this nickel-iron fluid are the main source of Earth's magnetic field. Inside the outer core that field averages about 2.5 millitesla, 50 times stronger than at the surface. The field protects life from interplanetary radiation and keeps the solar wind from stripping away the atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Heat and chemistry drive the motion
paragraphs.text: The churning is driven by heat and also by chemistry. Light elements pushed out of the inner core float up through the liquid while denser ones sink, and this releases gravitational energy that powers the geodynamo, the process that makes Earth's magnetic field. Rough estimates credit this chemical mixing with about 80 percent of the geodynamo's power and heat with about 20 percent.

paragraphs.heading: Lighter than pure iron
paragraphs.text: Pure iron or an iron-nickel alloy would be denser than measurements show the outer core to be. In fact it is about 5 to 10 percent less dense than iron would be at its temperature and pressure. So scientists propose that light elements, those with low atomic numbers, make up part of it. Nobody can sample it directly, but high-pressure experiments, calculations from seismic data, models of Earth's growth, and comparisons with meteorites narrow the options. By weight, estimates from 2023 give it about 5 percent nickel, 1.7 percent sulfur, as much as 5.3 percent oxygen and 4 percent silicon, and small amounts of carbon and hydrogen.

paragraphs.heading: A slowly freezing core
paragraphs.text: As the core cools, liquid at the bottom of the outer core freezes onto the inner core. The inner core grows by an estimated 1 mm a year this way, which adds up to about 80,000 tonnes of iron every second. The cooling rate is uncertain, but one estimate says the core should not freeze solid for about 91 billion years. That is long after the Sun is expected to swell, sterilize Earth's surface and burn out.
